#9687. Dharma Field Extractor: Any Document In, Structured Fields in JSON Out

A 2-billion-parameter model that extracts exactly the fields you ask for, from any document type, outperforming every frontier LLM we tested, at a fraction of the cost.

In April, we released DharmaOCR-LITE, a model specialized for OCR across a wide range of documents, from contracts and court filings to invoices, IDs and forms. The paper behind it made a narrow, well-measured case for domain specialization: a smaller model trained closer to its task beating general-purpose frontier APIs on that task.

OCR gives you the text on a page, faithful to the original formatting. That's exactly what you want when the job is the whole document, like a contract you'll read end to end or a manuscript you're digitizing.

However, there's a different use case: you don't want the page, you want specific fields out of it, in a shape a system downstream can consume. Every line item on an invoice, as a list. The patient name, exam type and date from a medical requisition, ready to schedule. The fields off an ID, mapped to the columns of an employee record.

Run that document through OCR and you get back everything printed on it, line by line, with no indication of which string is the exam type, which is the date or which number is the total. Someone still has to write the code that maps each value to the right field before it reaches the database.

A general-purpose LLM can do this work today, with careful prompting. At frontier API pricing and latency, on a task many businesses need to run at high volume, that quickly becomes the expensive way to solve a well-defined problem.

So we built a model for it instead. The Field Extractor takes a document image and either a request for everything it can find, or an exact schema to fill, and returns structured JSON: typed, field by field, nested where the document nests. An invoice comes back with every line item as an ordered list, each with its own quantity and value, alongside the totals. An ID comes back as the fields you'll store, under the names your system already uses for them. The same checkpoint handles all of it, with no per-type fine-tuning.

Say a batch of supplier invoices lands every morning, and you need four things off each one to push into your system: the supplier, the invoice number, the due date, the total. Same story for medical requisitions going into a scheduler, or contracts feeding a compliance system, where what matters is the parties, the term, the penalties and the fine amounts. You don't need the page, you need certain fields. With the Field Extractor there are two ways to ask for them:

The choice comes down to what you already know. Send an open request when you don't know what the document holds. Send a schema when the output has to match a shape that already exists somewhere else.

Either way, what comes back is JSON: the fields as keys, the values typed as requested, and null where the document didn't have what you asked for. When you send a schema, the output follows it exactly, with the same keys and no extra fields, so it can go straight into the next system.

The base model is DharmaOCR-LITE v1.1, a new 2-billion-parameter version optimized from the one in the paper and already specialized for OCR through supervised fine-tuning and DPO. On top of that checkpoint we trained a LoRA adapter on 43,384 training examples covering both request modes.

The data is organized into three streams:

All three streams are annotated at the field level. The mix is deliberately multi-domain: receipts, commercial invoices, forms, bank statements, ID documents and synthetic documents, rather than one filing type.

The full benchmark covers 546 documents across three request scenarios, for 1,638 total cases: extracting every field with no schema, a partial schema naming only real fields, and a schema that also includes deliberately nonexistent fields. The score is field-level F1 (matched by path, including position inside a table), multiplied by the Levenshtein similarity on the values that matched and by the share of outputs that come back as valid JSON.

We ran the same benchmark against four general-purpose frontier configurations.

Against general-purpose LLMs, the quality gap runs from 1.8 points (Claude Opus 5, the closest) to 9.3 points (GPT-5.6 Luna, the widest).

Cost runs from roughly 6 times lower (GPT-5.6 Luna) to roughly 147 times lower (GPT-5.6 Sol). The two sides are priced differently. The frontier figures come from measured average input and output tokens per page, reasoning tokens included, against each provider's published list pricing. Every frontier model ran with reasoning set to low; Claude Opus 5 used adaptive effort, which can skip reasoning on simpler pages while staying at the low level. Ours isn't billed per token: the model runs self-hosted, so the figure is GPU time on a single L40S at $2.24 per hour.

This is not a sales price. Self-hosted cost depends on the hardware, the volume and the latency each deployment needs. The comparison is here to show that a sovereign SSLM, deployed on your own infrastructure, is a real alternative to frontier APIs.

SROIE and FUNSD are two public datasets in our benchmark, not used in training. Below is one example from each.

On a SROIE receipt, we asked for all 18 fields printed on it, with no phantom fields this time, and every one comes back correct: the multi-line, unlabeled billing address captured as a single field, the two blank fields (salesperson and ref) correctly returned as null, and every number on the receipt matching to the cent.

On a FUNSD photocopying variance form, a checklist of twelve boolean fields with one nested group of five sub-options, the model marks exactly the one box that's checked (poor quality original, with a handwritten "faded" note beside it) as true, and the other eleven as false, matching the form exactly. It also reads the handwritten Bates ID off the page correctly, and returns null for the two fields left blank.

A 2-billion-parameter model scored 0.834, above every frontier configuration we tested, from Claude Opus 5 at 0.816 to GPT-5.6 Luna at 0.741, while running on a single L40S at a lower cost per extraction than every API in the comparison. Higher quality and lower cost, measured on the same benchmark, in the same run.

This isn't the first time we've measured it. Our OCR paper put the first DharmaOCR-LITE, a 3-billion-parameter model, above every commercial frontier API tested on Brazilian Portuguese; three months later, newer and better-resourced models arrived, and the gap held. Now a 2-billion-parameter model does it on field extraction. Each result adds evidence for the thesis we started Dharma-AI with: on a bounded task, a small model trained close to that task beats a frontier model asked to do the same thing in general. In this benchmark, it also cost 6 to 147 times less to run.

Parameter count sets the ceiling; training decides how much of it a model reaches on your task. Your business doesn't need the biggest model available. It needs one trained for your problem.

#9686. 5 Common Prescription Drugs Linked To Memory Loss

Prescription drugs taken by millions of people around the world can affect memory.

Prescription drugs taken by millions of people around the world can affect memory.

Memory loss is not always a result of ageing.

Here are five types of drugs that can affect memory.

The older type of antidepressants — known as tricyclics — have been linked to memory loss.

Around half of people taking them report problems concentrating and one-third say they have memory loss.

Benzodiazepines include drugs marketed under the names Valium, Ativan, Klonopin and Xanax.

These drugs are often prescribed for anxiety and other mental health issues such as OCD, insomnia and post-traumatic stress disorder.

Unfortunately they are also linked to memory loss and even Alzheimer’s.

Dr Helene Alphonso, a psychiatrist and Director of Osteopathic Medical Education at Texas University, said:

“Current research is extremely clear and physicians need to partner with their patients to move them into therapies, like [modern] anti-depressants, that are proven to be safer and more effective.”

Statins are prescribed to many people to keep their cholesterol in a safer range.

The Food and Drug Administration lists memory loss, forgetfulness and confusion as possible side-effects of the drug.

Some people do report memory problems when taking them, but the studies conducted so far are inconclusive.

Beta-blockers slow the heart rate and are used to lower blood pressure.

They are also prescribed to those with congestive heart problems.

Beta-blockers, though, may also cause the loss of emotional memories.

They have even been tested as a way of treating post-traumatic stress disorder because of their ability to block emotional memories.

Again, though, the studies are not conclusive.

People who cannot sleep are sometimes prescribed so-called ‘Z-drugs’.

The ‘Z-drugs’ have been linked to memory loss: especially losing the ability to make new memories.

They have also been reported to cause strange behaviours like driving or cooking with absolutely no memory of the event.

Where possible consider a psychological therapy or applicable alternative to using these drugs.

Naturally, you should always consult your physician before making changes to your medication.

To see what's happening in docker, we have Docker Desktop. But what if your VPS runs docker, do we have a GUI for that ? So I recently set up Portainer on my Ubuntu VPS to manage Docker containers through a web-based interface. Instead of exposing the Portainer dashboard directly to the public internet, I decided to access it through an SSH tunnel.

Here's a quick walkthrough of how I got it working.

The first step was to make sure Docker was installed and running on my Ubuntu VPS.

Once that was ready, I pulled and started the Portainer Community Edition container:

After the container was running, I needed to complete Portainer's initial setup.

Portainer generates a setup token that can be retrieved from the container logs:

I copied the setup token and used it during the initial setup process in further steps.

Instead of opening port 9443 to the entire internet, I created an SSH tunnel from my local machine to the VPS.

Keep this SSH session running in the background of your terminal.

Now, whenever I want to access Portainer, I simply open the following URL in my local browser:

And that's it! I'm now accessing the Portainer dashboard running on my remote Ubuntu VPS, directly from my local machine.

One thing worth noting is that Portainer's web interface listens on port 9443 using HTTPS by default.

Since I'm accessing it through SSH tunnelling, I don't need to expose the dashboard publicly.

When you access the portainer dashboard for the first time, it will ask you to create a user (admin by default) and a password.

Setup a secure password and paste the setup_token that we copied in step 2.

A small but important tip: Save this password in a password manager like Bitwarden. It's much better than storing it in a text file or relying on memory.

I like this setup because I don't have to expose another administrative dashboard to the public internet.

One security note: Make sure port 9443 is blocked from public access in your VPS firewall or cloud firewall. The Docker port mapping can expose a port independently of some UFW rules, so verify the actual network accessibility rather than relying on UFW alone.

Also, remember that mounting /var/run/docker.sock gives Portainer extensive control over Docker on the VPS, so keep its administrator credentials secure.

That's how I got Portainer running on my Ubuntu VPS and accessed it locally without making its dashboard publicly accessible. A simple combination of Docker, Portainer, and SSH tunnelling!

#9683. Most Frequently Asked Questions About Affiliate Marketing

Affiliate marketing is a way to make money by promoting the products and services of other people and companies. You don't need to create your product or service, just promote existing ones. That's why it's so easy to get started with affiliate marketing. You can even get started with no budget at all!

An affiliate program is a package of information you create for your product, which is then made available to potential publishers. The program will typically include details about the product and its retail value, commission levels, and promotional materials. Many affiliate programs are managed via an affiliate network like ShareASale, which acts as a platform to connect publishers and advertisers, but it is also possible to offer your program directly.

Affiliate networks connect publishers to advertisers.  Affiliate networks make money by charging fees to the merchants who advertise with them; these merchants are known as advertisers. The percentage of each sale that the advertiser pays is negotiated between the merchant and the affiliate network.

Dropshipping is a method of selling that allows you to run an online store without having to stock products. You advertise the products as if you owned them, but when someone makes an order, you create a duplicate order with the distributor at a reduced price. The distributor takes care of the post and packaging on your behalf. As affiliate marketing is based on referrals and this type of drop shipping requires no investment in inventory when a customer buys through the affiliate link, no money exchanges hands.

Performance marketing is a method of marketing that pays for performance, like when a sale is made or an ad is clicked This can include methods like PPC (pay-per-click) or display advertising. Affiliate marketing is one form of performance marketing where commissions are paid out to affiliates on a performance basis when they click on their affiliate link and make a purchase or action.

Smartphones are essentially miniature computers, so publishers can display the same websites and offers that are available on a PC. But mobiles also offer specific tools not available on computers, and these can be used to good effect for publishers. Publishers can optimize their ads for mobile users by making them easy to access by this audience. Publishers can also make good use of text and instant messaging to promote their offers. As the mobile market is predicted to make up 80% of traffic in the future, publishers who do not promote on mobile devices are missing out on a big opportunity.

The best way to find affiliate publishers is on reputable networks like ShareASale Cj(Commission Junction), Awin, and Impact radius. These networks have a strict application process and compliance checks, which means that all affiliates are trustworthy.

An affiliate disclosure statement discloses to the reader that there may be affiliate links on a website, for which a commission may be paid to the publisher if visitors follow these links and make purchases.

Publishers promote their programs through a variety of means, including blogs, websites, email marketing, and pay-per-click ads. Social media has a huge interactive audience, making this platform a good source of potential traffic.

A super affiliate is an affiliate partner who consistently drives a large majority of sales from any program they promote, compared to other affiliate partners involved in that program.  Affiliates make a lot of money from affiliate marketing Pat Flynn earned more than $50000 in 2013 from affiliate marketing.

Because the Internet is so widespread, affiliate programs can be promoted in any country. Affiliate strategies that are set internationally need to be tailored to the language of the targeted country.

Affiliate marketing can help you grow your business in the following ways:

One of the best ways to work with qualified affiliates is to hire an affiliate marketing agency that works with all the networks. Affiliates are carefully selected and go through a rigorous application process to be included in the network.

Affiliate marketing is generally associated with websites, but there are other ways to promote your affiliate links, including:

To build your affiliate marketing business, you don't have to invest money in the beginning. You can sign up for free with any affiliate network and start promoting their brands right away.

Commission rates are typically based on a percentage of the total sale and in some cases can also be a flat fee for each transaction. The rates are set by the merchant.

Some merchants run their affiliate programs internally, while others choose to contract out management to a network or an external agency.

#9682. How to Optimize Resume Bullets: Verbs + Numbers

Posted on Nov 5 • Originally published at all-done.xyz

Disclosure: I am the maker of all-done.xyz, a free collection of online tools. This post is a cross-post of a guide I wrote there, rewritten here in fresh words.

Most resumes read like a list of duties. Hiring managers, though, are not really shopping for duties — they are looking for proof. A bullet that only says what you were assigned to do leaves the reader guessing. A bullet that shows what changed because of your work answers the question for them.

A useful way to shape each bullet is to open with a precise action word, name the scope of the work, and finish with a measurable result. Instead of saying you handled a process, say what you did to it and what improved: time saved, costs cut, revenue added, complaints reduced, or users reached.

Verb choice also helps with screening software. Applicant tracking systems look for concrete language, and a vague opener such as "helped with" or "worked on" gives them very little to match. Pick verbs that fit the story: words that signal leadership when you led something, words that signal results when you moved a number, and words that signal problem-solving when you fixed or simplified something.

Almost every role has countable evidence hiding in plain sight. Count the people you supported, the tickets you closed in a week, the reports you shipped each month, the budget you managed, or the size of the audience you served. When an exact figure is not available, a fair range or a clear scale still beats no number at all. You can also borrow context from the business around you, such as the size of the team or the volume of work your group handled.

Read each bullet and ask one question: does it prove something, or only describe a task? If it only describes a task, add the action you took and the result that followed. Swap tired verbs for sharper ones, cut filler, and keep each bullet to one clear achievement. Three to five strong bullets for a recent role usually say more than a long list of duties.

If you want a head start, try the free tools below — no signup is needed:

The full guide is on my site: How to Optimize Resume Bullets: Verbs + Numbers.

#9679. Why Faster Coding Still Leads to Late Releases: A 90-Day Engineering Reset

AI tools can help developers produce code faster. Yet a team can finish more pull requests, run successful demos, and still struggle to explain which features customers will receive next.

That gap is the central topic of Faster Code, Late Releases: The 90-Day Engineering Reset, an AI Thoughtmakers conversation published by GeekyAnts featuring Santhosh Murthy.

The discussion examines a familiar engineering problem: visible activity looks healthy while delivery remains unpredictable. Its proposed response is a focused reset of priorities, ownership, and working processes.

For developers and engineering leads, the useful starting point is understanding where work waits after the code has been written.

In the conversation, Murthy describes a team whose sprint planning, demos, and dashboards appeared healthy. The problem became visible when leadership asked what customers would receive by the end of the quarter.

A dashboard showing completed tasks or increased pull request activity answers questions about individual stages of development. It may leave the larger delivery question unresolved.

A feature can be implemented but still wait for review, integration, testing, or release coordination. Reporting the implementation as progress does not explain how much work remains before customers can use it.

A useful delivery discussion therefore connects each priority to three things:

Without that connection, teams can stay busy while commitments become increasingly difficult to predict.

One of the clearest examples in the transcript concerns pull request reviews.

Murthy explains that code creation previously consumed substantial time. As AI accelerated that stage, reviews became a more visible constraint.

He investigated the problem through conversations with engineers and an AI-assisted examination of six months of backlog history. Tickets spending extended periods in review supported the concerns raised by the team.

The lesson is specific: improving one stage does not establish that the entire delivery process has improved.

These questions help distinguish time spent actively progressing a change from time spent waiting.

They also make a process discussion more concrete than a general request for developers to work faster.

The transcript describes the first month as a period for understanding roadblocks while important delivery work continues.

A reset does not require every project to stop. Existing customer commitments still need attention, and leadership must decide which work deserves protection.

Murthy suggests asking engineers what repeatedly slows their work or wastes time each week.

Answers might reveal delayed reviews, unclear release schedules, conflicting team priorities, or uncertainty about ownership. In the example discussed, both review delays and release coordination emerged as concerns.

Those conversations should lead to a written account of the problem:

The purpose is to establish a shared understanding of the delivery problem before introducing another process.

Once blockers become visible, the reset needs decisions.

One recommendation in the conversation is to stop automatically accepting new work. That requires leadership to make explicit trade-offs.

For example, a team already handling four priorities cannot absorb a fifth without consequences. The decision should identify which existing commitment moves, which deadline changes, or which request waits.

Otherwise, the original priorities remain on paper while attention shifts elsewhere.

Ownership needs similar clarity. Each important feature should have someone accountable for coordinating its progress, dependencies, and unresolved decisions.

This does not mean one person performs every task. It means the team knows who can explain the feature’s status and move a blocked decision forward.

Murthy also emphasizes that disagreements deserve discussion, while an accountable product decision-maker must ultimately resolve competing priorities.

A reset becomes useful when those decisions change how work moves.

Priorities can become unstable when teams repeatedly revisit decisions without remembering why they were made.

The conversation recommends keeping a decision log with a story or feature. It records what was prioritized or deferred, when the decision happened, and the reasoning behind it.

Decision: Defer the reporting enhancement. Reason: The customer-facing release depends on completing the integration work first. Owner: Product lead. Revisit condition: Integration work reaches the agreed release milestone.

This illustrative format gives future discussions a starting point. A changed priority can then be assessed against changed circumstances.

The outcome described in the conversation is clarity.

Team members should understand their responsibilities, the features they support, and what those features will deliver to customers.

The habits that preserve that clarity include weekly priority checks, recorded decisions, and fewer meetings that interrupt focused work.

The discussion also identifies an ownership warning sign for startups: the same two or three people appear in every incident or release conversation while others lack context.

A useful reset distributes understanding as well as responsibility.

Faster coding creates an opportunity to improve delivery. Realizing that opportunity requires attention to the reviews, decisions, and handoffs that follow implementation.

#9675. Why Windows saves your JPEGs as .jfif, and the one registry value that fixes it

You right-click a photo in Chrome or Edge, choose Save image as, and Windows offers photo.jfif. Then the upload form at work, the visa portal or an older app says the file type is not allowed.

The file is fine. Here is what is going on and how to stop it.

JFIF (JPEG File Interchange Format) is the wrapper most .jpg files have always used. A .jfif and a .jpg from the same source both start with the bytes FF D8 FF E0, and a few bytes later the letters JFIF. Same format, different ending.

So for one file, renaming photo.jfif to photo.jpg is enough. Nothing is converted and nothing is lost.

When a browser saves a download whose type is image/jpeg, it asks Windows which file ending belongs to that type. Windows looks it up in the registry here:

The value named Extension holds the answer. On many machines it says .jfif: an app or an update set it at some point, and every browser on that machine follows it. You can check yours in PowerShell:

On the Windows 11 laptop I wrote this on, it printed .jfif.

Open PowerShell as administrator and run:

Close and reopen the browser. Save image as now offers .jpg.

If you cannot change the registry (a work laptop, a shared PC), renaming each file still works.

A folder full of .jfif files can be renamed with one line of PowerShell, run inside that folder:

Only the names change, so the pictures stay exactly the same.

For a phone, or when you just need a couple of files fixed in a browser, we made a small free tool that gives a .jfif the .jpg ending without saving the picture again, so it keeps all of its quality (it also takes out hidden details such as the location): JFIF to JPG. It works without an account.

#9674. Your AI says "fixed". Would a test notice if it wasn't?

When an AI coding tool says "Fixed, and I added a test", how do you know the test would catch the bug coming back?

Bite is a small free tool that checks. It takes each recent fix back out of your code and runs your tests. If they still pass, nothing guards that fix, and Bite names it. On real public projects, not a staged demo, it found a memory leak in prosemirror-py that a commit said it had fixed. The fix for it has since been merged there.

Try it, no key needed. It works on copies and never edits your code. With plain Python, two lines in any terminal: python -m pip install bite-check python -m bite_check --free It shows a demo on a made-up project first, then tells you how to check your own (drag its folder into the window). Have pipx or uv? pipx run bite-check --free or uvx bite-check --free.

Doing MLH Hack Week (Nov 6-12)? Bite has good first issues: small Python fixes, each with "where to look" and "done when". They get picked up fast, so the label always shows what's still open. Comment on one to claim it. https://github.com/connabyss/bite/labels/good%20first%20issue

So: which of your AI's "fixed" commits would you bet on? Run it and find out.

#9673. We Stopped Feeding LLMs Raw HTML: Cutting Agent Scraping Costs by 74% Across 10,000 Targets

Every AI agent demo looks the same. You pass a URL to a scraper, hand the returned text to a model, and get clean JSON back. It works beautifully — right up until you point it at the real internet.

We were building an autonomous agent to track enterprise GPU availability: H100, H200, and Blackwell server rentals across cloud providers, wholesale distributor dashboards, and secondary marketplace brokers. The goal was simple. Watch thousands of supply points, detect availability and price shifts, and flag them before competitors noticed.

It collapsed in four days. Not because the model was weak, but because the plumbing underneath it was naive. Three things broke at once.

Roughly 78% of our target portals sat behind Cloudflare Turnstile, DataDome, or Akamai. Headless Chromium containers looped on challenges until the concurrency pool drained into a wall of HTTP 403s. The agent wasn't slow. It was locked out.

Premium residential bandwidth runs $8 to $15 per gigabyte. Downloading hero images, web fonts, and analytics beacons across 10,000 hourly targets meant infrastructure cost more than the arbitrage margin we were chasing. A system that is profitable on paper and cash-negative in practice is not a product. It is an expensive hobby.

The lesson that reshaped the whole design: an agent cannot reason over data it cannot reach, and it cannot stay cheap if every fetch is a paid browser session.

Our original pipeline sent every request through a rotating proxy and a full headless render. That is paying premium prices to read public pages.

We replaced it with three tiers of escalation. The rule: escalate only when the previous tier actually fails.

Tier 0 — Direct HTTP/2 (free). An async request with browser-accurate TLS fingerprints. If the response is a 200 with no mitigation signatures, we take the payload and move on. Documentation endpoints, status feeds, older portals, sitemaps, and RSS all die here, at zero marginal cost.

Tier 2 — Bright Data Scraping Browser. Only about 14% of targets genuinely need client-side rendering: React and Vue dashboards that hydrate pricing tables over WebSockets after load. Instead of running Chromium locally, we connect to a cloud browser over CDP and block images, CSS, and fonts at the network interception layer before a single byte is downloaded.

That single decision — connect to a remote browser instead of spawning a local one — cut memory per worker from 640 MB to 38 MB, and it took fingerprint-based honeypots out of the equation entirely.

A 2.4 MB e-commerce page usually contains under 4 KB of useful data. We built a deterministic pre-processor with two stages.

Stage 1: JSON-LD harvester. Retailers expose schema.org product and price data for Google, so we read that first. About 320 tokens, zero LLM calls, no hallucination surface. If a valid schema exists, the model never runs at all.

The model receives structure, not noise. That is the difference between an extraction agent and an expensive random-text summarizer.

Benchmark: 10,000 bot-protected URLs over seven days, compared against a baseline of local Playwright plus generic rotating residential proxies.

Request success rate: 36.4% baseline, 99.4% with the tri-tier engine.

Median ingestion latency: 14.8 seconds down to 2.6 seconds.

Tokens per LLM call: 14,200 down to 1,650.

Cost per 10,000 operations: $184.20 down to $47.50.

The cost delta is the entire argument. At 100,000 daily checks, the naive stack burns roughly $1,842 a day before the model thinks once. Tri-tier routing is not a micro-optimization. It is the difference between a viable product and a money fire.

Production exposes what benchmarks hide. Three things we had to fix after launch.

Sticky session lockouts. Rotating IPs on every request invalidated multi-step carts and authenticated distributor portals. Fixed by pinning consistent session identifiers to the same residential exit node for the duration of a transaction.

Canvas fingerprinting. Newer anti-bot suites render interactive WebGL challenges that static scrapers cannot simulate. Offloading those specific endpoints to the cloud browser resolved it without touching the rest of the pipeline.

Failures that compound. Blind retries turned a single upstream outage into a request storm. Fixed with exponential backoff, jitter, and cached state snapshots so the agent degrades instead of collapsing.

The hard part of autonomous agents is not the prompt. It is the ingestion layer: reaching the data, paying the minimum for it, and delivering it clean enough that a model can reason about it without inventing things.

Treat extraction as production infrastructure, and your agent stops being a demo. Ignore it, and no amount of prompt engineering will save you — because the agent will be staring at a 403 page and hallucinating anyway.

#9672. TOP 11 AI MARKETING TOOLS YOU SHOULD USE (Updated 2022)

If you’re late to the AI party, don’t worry. It’s easier than you think to start leveraging artificial intelligence tools in your marketing strategy. Here are 11 AI marketing tools every marketer should start using today.

Personalize is an AI-powered technology that helps you identify and produce highly targeted sales and marketing campaigns by tracking the products and services your contacts are most interested in at any given time. The platform uses an algorithm to identify each contact’s top three interests, which are updated in real-time based on recent site activity.

Seventh Sense provides behavioral analytics that helps you win attention in your customers’ overcrowded email inboxes. Choosing the best day and time to send an email is always a gamble. And while some days of the week generally get higher open rates than others, you’ll never be able to nail down a time that’s best for every customer. Seventh Sense eases your stress of having to figure out the perfect send-time and day for your email campaigns. The AI-based platform figures out the best timing and email frequency for each contact based on when they’re opening emails. The tool is primarily geared toward HubSpot and Marketo customers

Phrasee uses artificial intelligence to help you write more effective subject lines. With its AI-based Natural Language Generation system, Phrasee uses data-driven insights to generate millions of natural-sounding copy variants that match your brand voice. The model is end-to-end, meaning when you feed the results back to Phrasee, the prediction model rebuilds so it can continuously learn from your audience.

HubSpot Search Engine Optimization (SEO) is an integral tool for the Human Content team. It uses machine learning to determine how search engines understand and categorize your content. HubSpot SEO helps you improve your search engine rankings and outrank your competitors. Search engines reward websites that organize their content around core subjects, or topic clusters. HubSpot SEO helps you discover and rank for the topics that matter to your business and customers.

When you’re limited to testing two variables against each other at a time, it can take months to get the results you’re looking for. Evolv AI lets you test all your ideas at once. It uses advanced algorithms to identify the top-performing concepts, combine them with each other, and repeat the process to achieve the best site experience.

Acrolinx is a content alignment platform that helps brands scale and improves the quality of their content. It’s geared toward enterprises – its major customers include big brands like Google, Adobe, and Amazon - to help them scale their writing efforts. Instead of spending time chasing down and fixing typos in multiple places throughout an article or blog post, you can use Acrolinx to do it all right there in one place. You start by setting your preferences for style, grammar, tone of voice, and company-specific word usage. Then, Acrolinx checks and scores your existing content to find what’s working and suggest areas for improvement. The platform provides real-time guidance and suggestions to make writing better and strengthen weak pages.

MarketMuse uses an algorithm to help marketers build content strategies. The tool shows you where to target keywords to rank in specific topic categories, and recommends keywords you should go after if you want to own particular topics. It also identifies gaps and opportunities for new content and prioritizes them by their probable impact on your rankings. The algorithm compares your content with thousands of articles related to the same topic to uncover what’s missing from your site.

Copilot is a suite of tools that help eCommerce businesses maintain real-time communication with customers around the clock at every stage of the funnel. Promote products, recover shopping carts and send updates or reminders directly through Messenger.

Yotpo’s deep learning technology evaluates your customers’ product reviews to help you make better business decisions. It identifies key topics that customers mention related to your products—and their feelings toward them. The AI engine extracts relevant reviews from past buyers and presents them in smart displays to convert new shoppers. Yotpo also saves you time moderating reviews. The AI-powered moderation tool automatically assigns a score to each review and flags reviews with negative sentiment so you can focus on quality control instead of manually reviewing every post.

Albert is a self-learning software that automates the creation of marketing campaigns for your brand. It analyzes vast amounts of data to run optimized campaigns autonomously, allowing you to feed in your own creative content and target markets, and then use data from its database to determine key characteristics of a serious buyer. Albert identifies potential customers that match those traits, and runs trial campaigns on a small group of customers—with results refined by Albert himself—before launching it on a larger scale.

Albert plugs into your existing marketing technology stack, so you still have access to your accounts, ads, search, social media, and more. Albert maps tracking and attribution to your source of truth so you can determine which channels are driving your business.

There are many tools and companies out there that offer AI tools, but this is a small list of resources that we have found to be helpful. If you have any other suggestions, feel free to share them in the comments below this article. As marketing evolves at such a rapid pace, new marketing strategies will be invented that we haven't even dreamed of yet. But for now, this list should give you a good starting point on your way to implementing AI into your marketing mix.

#9671. ADHD-Friendly Firefox Setup: Reducing Browser Distraction Surfaces

People with ADHD often develop elaborate systems to manage attention, context-switching, and task completion. The browser is where a lot of that system lives — and a poorly configured browser can make ADHD harder to manage, while a well-configured one can meaningfully help.

Here's what works, based on the specific challenges ADHD creates in a browser environment.

Opening tabs is easy. Closing them feels like losing something — what if you need that article later? The result is hundreds of open tabs, most of which will never be read again, creating visual overwhelm and slowing down everything.

The real fix is accepting that you won't get back to most of those tabs and building a habit around it. But the browser can help:

Tab Groups (available in Firefox via settings) let you collapse related tabs into a named group. Research tabs for one topic collapse into a small label. This reduces the visual noise without requiring you to close things.

OneTab extension (Firefox, Chrome) lets you send all current tabs to a saved list with one click. Everything closes. The list is there if you need to recover something. Using this aggressively at the end of each session removes accumulated tab debt.

Auto Tab Discard suspends tabs that haven't been used in a while, reducing memory usage without closing them. This helps if you have many tabs open but only actively use a few.

The new tab is a vulnerability for ADHD brains. Opening a new tab to do something specific — search for a thing, navigate somewhere — and then getting caught by a news headline, a trending video, or social media notifications is a common ADHD pattern.

The fix: replace the new tab with something that has no distraction content.

Weather & Clock Dashboard shows weather and world clocks on the new tab. It's information, not engagement. There's no feed, no headlines, no "you might also like." You open a new tab, see the time and weather, and proceed to what you were doing.

This sounds small but it matters: the new tab is opened constantly, and removing the distraction bait from it removes many small diversions per day.

Browser notifications are a persistent ADHD trigger. Sites request permission to send notifications, you say yes during a moment of optimism, and they deliver a constant stream of interruptions.

Firefox doesn't have a built-in focus mode, but you can create one using containers. Create a "Focus" container with only the tabs you need for your current task. Keep your email and social media in a separate container that you close entirely during deep work.

This isn't perfect — you can still navigate to distracting sites — but the friction of switching containers provides a small but meaningful pause before distraction happens.

When you've navigated away from your work and need to get back: Ctrl+1 through Ctrl+8 jump to pinned tabs by position. Pin your three most important work tabs. When you notice you've drifted, one keystroke gets you back without having to scan through open tabs.

Ctrl+Shift+T reopens the most recently closed tab. For the specific ADHD pattern of "I accidentally closed the thing I was working on" — this is the fix.

Reader View (F9 in Firefox on eligible articles) strips everything except the article text. No sidebar links, no related articles, no ads, no floating share buttons. For people who get distracted mid-article by surrounding content, this significantly improves reading completion.

These don't cure ADHD. They reduce the number of times the browser actively works against attention by offering distraction surfaces. The fewer attention traps in your environment, the more capacity is available for actual work.

#9670. The best apples for apple pie: Here's how to choose.: We put six varieties to the test.

Which are the best pie apples? With apple-picking season hard upon us, it's time to dust off your favorite apple pie recipe, sharpen your crust-rolling skills, and get ready to enjoy fall's favorite dessert: apple pie.

You may be tempted to make your pie from one of the six apple varieties that dominate the domestic market year-round: Red Delicious, Golden Delicious, Gala, Fuji, Granny Smith, and McIntosh.

But when fall rolls around, farmers' markets and orchard farm stands offer an abundance of apple choices.

You've probably identified your favorite eating apple. But what about the best pie apples? They're not necessarily the same. Red and Golden Delicious, for instance, are reliably crisp, sweet-eating apples. But when you bake them into a pie, they can become mushy and lose some of their sweetness. So what are the best apples for pie?

We'll put six different pie apples to the test.

The pie apples: I decide to put two of my favorites, Golden Russet and Northern Spy, up against a couple of classic pie apples: McIntosh and Cortland. I also add Granny Smith because, if there's one ubiquitous, year-round apple, Granny Smith is it. Ginger Gold — a Golden Delicious cross with Albemarle Pippin — is another variety that's often available in fall, and a worthy representative of the Delicious family.

And yes, there are plenty of other apple varieties to choose from: Fuji, Gala, Honey Crisp, and so many more. But with limited time and resources — and a pan with space for just six pies — I'm not able to test every apple out there. But if you want to choose the best pie apples among your personal favorites, you can have fun doing this same test at home.

I use a muffin tin to bake apples sweetened with a bit of sugar. To mimic apple pie (sans crust), I pile sliced apples high in the pan. Then I bake them in a preheated 425°F oven for 20 minutes, lower the oven temperature to 375°F, and continue to bake the apples until they're bubbly, about 40 minutes.

I had no idea there'd be such significant differences in both texture and flavor. For example, Russets and Macs are sweetened with the same amount of sugar, bake at the same temperature, for the same amount of time —  and offer way different results.

So, Granny Smith looks like the best combination of both taste and texture. Does it make the very best apple pie?

Not necessarily. I've baked many pies with this all-purpose apple, especially during the winter when other apples are scarce or pricey. A pie made 100% with Granny Smith apples is a mighty fine pie. But in fall, when every apple variety in the world is seemingly at your fingertips, why not take advantage of one or two (or more) of your own local favorites?

At the end of the day, choosing the best pie apples is a personal decision. My best apple pie would include a combination of these three: Cortland, for flavor; Russet, for texture; and Granny Smith, for its combination of the two.

What apples would fill your best pie? Bake your favorite varieties side by side and see what happens; the results may surprise you.

Please share your favorite apples for pie — and your favorite apple pie tips! — in comments, below.

#9668. Stop Trusting Notification URLs

Hichem Hannafi is a Las Vegas–based technology entrepreneur with over 13 years of experience driving software innovation.

Hichem Hannafi is a Las Vegas–based technology entrepreneur with over 13 years of experience driving software innovation.

Hichem Hannafi is a Las Vegas–based technology entrepreneur with over 13 years of experience driving software innovation.

TL;DR: Every bid response a DSP sends carries URLs that anyone who has seen the response can call: impression, click, win, billing. Most DSPs count whatever comes in, which is where discrepancy reports come from. We treated a notification URL like a cheque: valid only if we issued it, for that bid, and it hasn’t been cashed. The bidder mints hashes and a spend reservation at bid time; every callback is checked against them, duplicates and replays are rejected, and unclaimed reservations expire after 45 minutes. Result: about 6% of callbacks rejected as unverifiable, and reported impressions within 1% of the exchanges’ figures.

Every bid response a DSP sends contains a set of URLs: call this one when the ad is shown, this one when it is clicked, this one when the auction is won, this one when it is billed. The exchange, the publisher’s page, and anyone else who has seen the response can call them. Most DSPs count whatever comes in.

That is the quiet reason discrepancy reports exist. Not fraud, usually, though fraud rides along happily. Mostly it is duplicate calls, replayed calls, calls from cached responses that never rendered, and callbacks for auctions the DSP did not win. Every one of them becomes an impression in a report, a dollar in an invoice, and an argument with an advertiser.

When I built the bidder for Mobinner’s DSP, I treated a notification URL the way a bank treats a cheque: it is only good if we issued it, for that amount, and it has not been cashed already.

The mechanism is simple. When a bidder node decides to bid, it does three things before it responds. It reserves the bid amount against the campaign budget in a shared store, so that parallel nodes cannot spend the same dollar twice. It generates a set of hashes, one for the conversion and one for each tracking event, and stores them alongside the reservation. And it embeds those hashes in the notification URLs it returns.

When a callback arrives, the handler does not count it. It looks up the hashes for that bid and compares. If they match, the event is written to reporting, the hash is cleared so the same event cannot be counted twice, and the spend is committed. If they do not match, or there is no reservation, the call is rejected, and nothing is recorded. If no callback ever arrives, the reservation expires after 45 minutes, and a cleaner service returns the budget to the campaign; conversion hashes live 48 hours, because conversions arrive late.

The result is that a notification URL has no value to anyone except the winner of the bid it was issued for, and that nothing reaches a report unless it was bid for, won, and seen once.

A write to the shared store on every bid, and a read on every callback. That is not free at scale, and it is the reason some DSPs skip it: the bid path is where milliseconds matter, and a store round trip is a visible cost. We judged it worth paying, because the alternative is reconciling discrepancies by hand every month, which costs more and never ends. In a typical month, we rejected roughly 6% of incoming callbacks as unverifiable, and our reported impressions came within 1% of the exchanges’ own figures.

Three things have changed since this design was new. Supply-path optimisation means a DSP sees the same impression through several paths, and duplicate callbacks are a feature of the plumbing, not a bug. Server-side rendering and prefetching mean more responses are generated than are ever shown. And the gap between a bid and its billing notice is where most of the money in programmatic goes missing.

A DSP that counts callbacks on trust is making a promise to advertisers it cannot keep. The fix is not a fraud vendor bolted on afterwards; it is refusing, at the point of counting, to count anything you did not issue.

Ask your DSP one question: if I call your impression URL twice, what happens? If the answer is anything other than “the second call is rejected,” you are paying for the second call.

Hichem Hannafi is a Las Vegas–based technology entrepreneur with over 13 years of experience driving software innovation.

#9667. Five Checks Before You Import an AI Site Model into OpenRoads

Last month a colleague dropped a folder on our server with a GenAnywhere export and a note that said site context, ready to use. I opened the mesh, looked at it for a minute, and did not touch it again for three days. Not because it was bad. Because I had not checked it yet.

This is the list I run before any AI-generated site model goes into an OpenRoads file. It takes about an hour. It has caught a wrong vertical datum twice this year and a units problem once.

Start with the file format and the coordinate system. The viewer does not care where the model sits. OpenRoads does. Ask which coordinate system the export uses, and whether the numbers are feet or meters. A model in state plane feet imported as meters will look plausible and be wrong by a factor of 3.28.

Measure a road width you can see on imagery. A two-lane road with shoulders is roughly 30 to 40 feet. If the model says 120, you have a units problem, not a wide road. If the file arrives as LandXML, open the header before you open the surface.

AI models often sit on a smooth global terrain, and the elevation may be relative, ellipsoidal, or simply offset. Check the minimum and maximum against a benchmark you trust. A site at 620 feet NAVD88 should not import at 1,840.

Pick a spot with a known elevation, usually a manhole rim or a surveyed benchmark. Compare. If the difference is constant, you can shift the model. If it changes across the site, the surface is not usable for design.

A mesh is not a TIN surface. It has triangles, but it does not know which edges matter. Walls, curbs, ditch bottoms, and top of bank are all inferred. Sometimes the inference is fine. Sometimes it cuts a corner through a retaining wall and nobody notices until the cross sections look strange. OpenRoads wants a breakline wherever the ground changes direction sharply, and the generated model rarely has one.

Turn on triangle edges and look for long skinny triangles crossing a road or a wall. Those are the places the surface is guessing. On a bridge job last winter, the mesh ran a single triangle from the deck edge to the creek bed. The deck looked fine in 3D and the profile was wrong by two feet at the abutment.

Check scale with two points you can measure on the ground, not with the viewer zoom. If the model is off by one percent over a mile, that is 52 feet. GIS data is often close enough for context and not close enough for design. If the source was a point cloud, ask how it was decimated, because decimation can move a curb.

The list is short and expensive: utilities, walls, culverts, inlets, guardrail, and anything underground. On a warehouse project, the generated model had the building and the parking but not the dock heights. We design to the dock, so the model was context, not a base. The same thing happens with drainage. A low spot in a parking lot is easy to see in a render and easy to miss in a mesh.

I keep a small script that reads an exported point file and prints the elevation range and a count of impossible values. It is not validation. It is a smoke test that catches the obvious failures before they reach a design file. The automation is deliberately dumb, because dumb checks are easy to trust.

For a public meeting or a quick visual, I skip all of this. The model goes into a viewer, not a design file. The checks exist for the moment someone says ready to use. That phrase is the trigger. A quality check is cheaper than a redesign, and a file format note in the project log is cheaper still. If the model fails two checks, I stop and ask for the source. There is no point patching a surface that was never measured.

#9664. Giving a macOS App Group Its Own Dock Icon: Design Lessons From Cybokron Dock Groups

Developer of Cybokron Dock Groups, a free and open-source macOS utility. https://cybokron.com/dock-groups/

Developer of Cybokron Dock Groups, a free and open-source macOS utility. https://cybokron.com/dock-groups/

Developer of Cybokron Dock Groups, a free and open-source macOS utility. https://cybokron.com/dock-groups/

A group of applications is easy to describe and surprisingly awkward to represent in a desktop interface. A developer might need an editor, a terminal, and a browser together, yet the Dock presents them as separate applications. Cybokron Dock Groups treats that collection as a named unit: something that can have its own icon, open its members, or hide them together. The interesting engineering problem is not the list of apps. It is making the group fit macOS without pretending it is a separate desktop session.

Disclosure: I am Ercan Atay, the developer of Cybokron Dock Groups, and have a direct interest in the project. This article was prepared with AI drafting assistance based on the project's public documentation. It is a developer's technical explanation, not an independent product review.

Consider a hypothetical Development group containing an editor, a terminal, a browser, and a documentation website. Opening that group should have a narrow, predictable meaning. It should launch applications that are closed, bring running applications forward, and open the website in the default browser.

It should not imply that a terminal command will resume, that a browser tab will return to a specific state, or that every window will move to a particular display. Those are different problems. Keeping that boundary explicit avoids promising a workspace-restoration system when the underlying object is a collection of launch targets.

The same distinction matters for ending work. Hide All hides only running member applications; it does not launch closed ones. Close All asks the group's running applications to quit normally. Force quit is a separate action, available through Command-click. It is not interchangeable with hiding, and it can discard unsaved work.

That gives the group a small vocabulary rather than a vague “switch workspace” command. The vocabulary is easier to explain because each action has a separate consequence.

A group can live in a menu-bar menu, but a persistent Dock entry needs something macOS can recognize. Cybokron's standalone mode creates a small application bundle for each group.

The bundle lives under the user's Application Support directory. It contains a copy of the project's executable, its own Info.plist, a group-specific bundle identifier, a group-config.json resource, and the group's icon. The executable runs in an agent role rather than creating another full menu-bar instance.

This is not just an alias to a list. The group has an application identity that can be registered with LaunchServices. Clicking its Dock icon toggles the popup; Option-click opens the group's members. The standalone agent can do this even when the main menu-bar app is not running.

There is a cost to that independence. A changed group needs its generated bundle updated, and a running agent needs to reload its configuration. A renamed group also needs its bundle path and Dock entry updated. The project repository documents these mechanics, including ad hoc signing and verification of the generated agents. These generated bundles should not be confused with the Developer ID-signed main application.

Adding a generated application to the Dock means changing persistent Dock entries. In this implementation, the Dock briefly restarts to display the change. That is a real side effect, not something a utility should conceal behind a claim of seamlessness.

The project keeps backups of the Dock's application list before writing it and retains the newest six. If it cannot read the existing list, it does not rewrite the Dock or disable groups on that basis. This is an important failure boundary: inability to understand an existing user configuration should not become permission to replace it.

The broader lesson is to design the failure path alongside the feature. A Dock icon is convenient, but preserving the user's existing Dock is more important than successfully adding one more item.

Apple's NSWorkspace documentation describes native facilities for launching applications and opening URLs. Those facilities are useful building blocks, but they do not make every piece of desktop interaction permission-free.

Cybokron asks for Accessibility access for global keyboard shortcuts, restoring minimized windows, and positioning a popup relative to its Dock icon. Without that permission, the remaining functionality is still available. Its global shortcuts are observed rather than consumed, so the foreground application also receives the key press.

That last detail is a trade-off worth stating plainly. A shortcut that works globally can still interact with the application currently in front. Users need to be able to change or disable it, not merely accept a hard-coded combination.

The same group operations are available through the cybokrondockgroups URL scheme. With a group named Work already configured, these examples show the distinction between displaying it and launching its members:

Apple's guide to using app URL schemes in Shortcuts explains how this kind of interface can connect an app to a larger workflow.

But a command URL is not equivalent to a private button. Another application or webpage can invoke it. Cybokron therefore asks for confirmation before a quit request, while launch and hide links share a five-second rate limit. These controls reduce specific accidental or repeated actions; they are not a claim that every possible external-input risk has disappeared.

Groups, settings, and usage counts stay in the user's Library folder. There is no account requirement or analytics service. However, the application does contact GitHub for release checks, release notes, and update downloads. Describing it as entirely offline would be inaccurate.

Update verification is also more than comparing a version string. The documented checks include the download's size and SHA-256, with Developer ID builds additionally requiring the expected signing identity. Older ad hoc-signed releases have a weaker trust boundary, so that distinction belongs in technical documentation rather than being flattened into a universal security claim.

The product page describes a free, MIT-licensed utility for macOS 14 and later, supporting Apple Silicon and Intel. The reusable idea is narrower than a feature list: make the group a recognizable native object, distinguish actions with different consequences, and expose the limits of permissions, persistence, and external commands. That is a useful design checklist even for a developer who never installs this particular utility.

Disclosure: I develop Cybokron Dock Groups and have a direct interest in it. AI assisted the preparation of this article. No independent testing or benchmark results are claimed here.

#9663. Agent instructions that actually change behaviour

Posted on Nov 5 • Originally published at mahmadmanzoor.com

My global instruction file for Claude Code has a five-line rule about which model a subagent should run on. It changes how every session spends money, and a short test shows that it does. Most instruction files I read are the opposite: long lists of sensible advice with no visible effect on what the agent actually does.

The difference is not clever wording. It is whether each rule sits in a place where it can work, whether it has a trigger, and whether anyone tested it. This is how I decide all three.

Claude Code reads CLAUDE.md (or a repository's AGENTS.md) at the start of every session. Skills are folders with a SKILL.md file that load only when a task matches their description. Hooks are scripts the harness runs at fixed points, such as before a tool call, and the model does not get a vote on whether they run. CI runs after all of that, on every push.

The further down a rule sits, the harder it is to ignore.

The documentation is frank about the first layer: CLAUDE.md is context, not enforced configuration. The model reads it and usually follows it. "Usually" is fine for style and preferences. It is not fine for "never push to main" or "never print the production database URL". Those belong lower down.

Things that are true in every session and short enough to read in every session: the commands to build and test, where things live, conventions the code does not make obvious, and the few rules that apply to every task. Anthropic's docs suggest keeping each file under 200 lines; I aim for well under half that. Every line costs context in every session and competes with every other line for attention.

If more than one kind of agent works in the repository, AGENTS.md is the shared name that several tools read, and Claude Code can read it in place of CLAUDE.md. I keep one file rather than two copies that drift apart. Personal preferences that should follow me across every project, like the model rule below, go in the global file in my home directory instead of in any repository.

This is the model rule from my global file, exactly as it is:

Each of these reads well and changes little.

The same kinds of rule fail again and again. Adjectives without a check ("write clean, maintainable code") give the model nothing to do differently, because it already believes that is what it does. Rules deep in a long file lose to the code in front of the model. Two rules that disagree, like "keep changes minimal" and "fix any issues you notice", get settled in whichever direction the task leans. And a rule with no trigger, like "be careful with auth", never fires, because nothing tells the agent that this moment is the auth moment.

The rules that work read like small if-statements. When something specific happens, do one concrete thing, because of a reason the agent can use on cases the rule did not list. The model rule has all three: the trigger is work going to a subagent, the action is setting model on every Agent call, and the reason is cost, with examples for each tier. The reason matters more than it looks. Without it, an agent meeting an odd case has to guess; with it, it can work out what I wanted.

Negative rules work better with a replacement. "Do not use any" leaves the agent stuck when a type gets hard. "Do not use any; use unknown and narrow it" gives it somewhere to go.

Some knowledge is long and only sometimes needed: how to draw a diagram in the house style, how to cut a release, how the seed script expects a post to look. In CLAUDE.md it would cost context in every unrelated session. A skill holds it instead. Only the name and description are in context up front, and the body loads when a task matches.

The description is the trigger, so write it like a CLAUDE.md rule: what the skill does, then "use when" with the situations that should load it. A vague description means the skill never loads, and from the outside that looks exactly like a skill that does not work.

A hook is a script the harness runs at a fixed point. A PreToolUse hook on Bash receives each command as JSON on stdin before it runs. Exit code 0 lets it run. Exit code 2 blocks it and hands whatever the script wrote to stderr back to the agent. The model cannot argue its way past that, because the model is not the one running it.

A refusal with a reason ends the loop. A bare refusal starts one.

The stderr message is part of the design. A bare refusal makes the agent try variations of the same command. A refusal that says what to do instead ends the attempt. Be clear about what this hook is, too: a guard rail against mistakes, not a security boundary. A command could hide the push inside a script file. Anything that has to hold against a determined command belongs in permissions, or in credentials the agent simply does not have.

I do not trust a rule until I have watched it change behaviour. The test is a probe: a small task that should trigger the rule, run in a fresh headless session, and checked from the tool calls in the log rather than from the agent's own account of what it did.

A pure rename should go to haiku. If the probe prints null, the agent started a subagent without choosing a model, and the rule failed. (Older Claude Code versions named the tool Task, so adjust the filter if yours does.) I run each probe three times, because one pass can be luck. If a rule still fails after a rewrite, it is telling me it belongs lower in the stack: a hook, a subagent definition with model: in its frontmatter, or a CI check.

Probes also catch regressions. When I add a rule I re-run the old probes, because a new line can quietly weaken an old one.

The test for every line is the same: can I show a probe where removing it changes what the agent does? If I cannot, the line goes.

Claude Code hooks reference: Every hook event, its JSON input and what exit code 2 does for each one.

#9662. Your AI agent invents product rules. Make it establish context first.

Posted on Nov 5 • Originally published at thewebhig.hashnode.dev

You ask your AI agent for an account settings screen. It returns a grid of cards, a dark-mode toggle you never mentioned, and a "delete account" control sitting next to a harmless preference. You push back. The next prompt invents a different layout, and a social-login switch the product does not have.

The agent filled gaps. It treated guesses as product rules.

Design Decision Method's first step is there to stop that. Step 1, establish context, asks the agent to read the brief and the product you already have before it decides anything about layout.

It also asks the agent to keep what it knows separate from what it assumes, and not to invent rules or capabilities the product lacks.

That is the whole first step. No wireframe yet. No colour palette. A short read of the brief and the existing product, then an honest list of facts and assumptions.

Say you run a small product at example.com, and you ask your agent for the account settings screen. This is an illustration of how the procedure applies, not a case study or a measured result.

Without the method, the agent invents. It adds toggles, cards, and a delete path because those are familiar from other products.

With step 1 filled in first, the note might look like this:

Audience: Account holders who manage their own profile. Mostly people who signed up themselves.

Task and frequency: Change email or password occasionally. Review notification preferences rarely. Delete the account almost never.

Cost of a mistake: Medium for email or password (lockout or missed mail). High for delete or billing changes.

Known: The product has email, password, and three notification toggles. There is no social login. There is no team account.

Assumptions (marked): Offline use was not requested, so none is designed. Billing settings live elsewhere; this screen does not invent them.

Now the agent has somewhere to stop inventing. A dark-mode switch that was never in the product stays out. A delete control does not sit next to a low-cost preference just because other apps do that. Optional additions get labelled instead of smuggled in as facts.

The useful part is the split. "Known" comes from the brief, the code, or a screen you already have. "Assumed" is everything else, and it stays marked.

If the agent cannot ask about a gap that would change the design, list the assumption in the deliverable instead of quietly filling it. You can confirm, correct, or reject the guess before layout hardens around it.

Agents are good at completing patterns. They are less good at noticing that your product never offered the pattern. The screen looks finished, and the invented parts are hard to spot until you click them.

Establish context makes the first deliverable a short statement of who the screen is for, how often people use it, what a mistake costs, and which device they are on. Later steps build on that statement. Without it, they decorate a guess.

The method does not claim this saves time. That has not been measured. What it does give you is a place to catch invented rules before they become UI.

A small copy change does not need a long context note. The method is a shared procedure, not mandatory for every small edit. When the change could invent a capability, bury a costly action, or import another domain's conventions, spend the few lines.

The design record template has a short Context section for this: audience and roles, primary tasks and frequency, cost of error, device, known facts, and assumptions. Use as much of it as the change needs.

Establish context is step 1 of six: establish context, choose the visual system, map objects before layout, write a decision record, structure each view, then deliver and validate.

Design Decision Method is a lightweight design decision workflow for developers building interfaces with AI agents. It follows the open Agent Skills format and is MIT licensed. Install paths for Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI, and Codex are in the README.

#9661. WARN Act and Missing Notices — What to Do If You Never Got a Layoff Notice

Posted on Nov 5 • Originally published at layoffatlas.com

The whole point of the WARN Act is advance warning. When a covered employer plans a mass layoff or plant closing, it must give affected workers 60 days' notice before the job loss takes effect. So when the layoff arrives and no notice ever came, the natural question is: was that legal, and what can you do about it?

A missing notice is worth investigating, not assuming. Some employers genuinely owe no notice, some owe a shorter notice under an exception, and some simply broke the law.

Under the federal WARN Act, a covered employer must give written notice to three groups: the affected workers themselves (or their union representative, if unionized), the state dislocated worker unit, and the chief elected official of the local government where the layoff happens. That last part matters for your search: if workers were never told, the state unit may still hold a copy of the filing.

Coverage is not universal. The federal law generally applies to employers with 100 or more full-time employees, and only to plant closings affecting 50 or more workers or mass layoffs meeting the law's thresholds. Workers employed fewer than 6 months in the last 12 months, or averaging fewer than 20 hours a week, do not count toward those thresholds. Several states set lower bars through their own mini-WARN laws, so a layoff that escapes federal coverage may still be covered by state law.

Before concluding no notice was given, check the places a filing would appear:

The WARN Act allows shorter notice in three narrow situations: a faltering company actively seeking capital or business that would avoid the layoff, unforeseeable business circumstances, and a natural disaster. These exceptions reduce the notice period; they do not automatically excuse giving no notice at all. An employer invoking one must still give as much notice as practicable.

A business downturn alone is not automatically unforeseeable: courts distinguish sudden, unexpected events from a decline the employer watched coming for months.

The federal WARN Act has no government agency that investigates complaints on your behalf. Workers enforce it themselves, usually through a private lawsuit, often as a group action with coworkers in the same position. The standard remedy is back pay and benefits for each day of violation, up to 60 days, plus attorney's fees. Some state mini-WARN laws add penalties: California allows civil penalties, New Jersey requires severance pay, and Hawaii allows up to $500 per day.

A missing notice does not automatically mean 60 days of pay is coming. If the employer was too small, the layoff too small, or a genuine exception applied, the claim may fail. Conversely, a notice that was given but defective — wrong dates, missing required information, sent to the wrong recipient — can still support a claim.

Fresh data from Layoff Atlas shows 676 notices covering 64,762 reported workers in the current 90-day window, with 26 counts unavailable. California (20,969 workers) and Washington (17,320) together account for nearly three-fifths of that total, followed by Illinois (3,649), Texas (2,863), and Virginia (2,373). The heaviest upcoming week is the week of November 19, with 8,412 workers scheduled, followed by November 12 (7,578) and November 26 (6,032). These figures describe reported plans, not confirmed job losses.

If you were laid off without warning, start with the registry check and the written request to your employer. Those two steps cost nothing, create a paper trail, and tell you quickly whether you have a paperwork gap, a genuine exception, or a claim worth pursuing.
